tr.td: Utah real estate agent convicted of poisoning her husband with fentanyl, who had published a children's book about grief after his death
Eric Richins, 39, found dead at the family home near Park City, Utah, on 4 March 2022

content.p: Early on the morning of 4 March 2022, Kouri Richins called 911 from her home in Kamas, a small town outside Park City, Utah. "My husband is not breathing. He's cold," she told the operator. Eric Richins, 39, who ran his own masonry business and was the father of their three young sons, was dead in their bed. An autopsy found about five times the lethal amount of fentanyl in his blood, and the medical examiner said it was the illicit kind, not the medical grade.

A year later his widow published a picture book to help children cope with the loss of a parent and promoted it on local television. Two months after that she was arrested for his murder. On 16 March 2026 a Summit County jury convicted her of aggravated murder, of an earlier attempt on his life, and of insurance fraud and forgery. Prosecutors said she poisoned him for money and to start a new life with another man. On 13 May 2026, the day Eric Richins would have turned 44, Judge Richard Mrazik sentenced her to life in prison without parole. She maintains her innocence and has said she will appeal.

The couple married in 2013. Under their prenuptial agreement neither had any claim on businesses the other set up, with one exception: if Eric Richins died while they were still married, his business would pass to her. In 2019 Kouri Richins started her own company, buying homes, renovating them and selling them on.

According to prosecutors, she began taking money from her husband's accounts without his knowledge that same year. When he found out in 2020, they said, he went to an estate-planning lawyer and set up a living trust that would put his sister Katie Richins-Benson in charge of his estate if he died. His wife was not told. Court filings said he later tried to take her off his life insurance and out of his will, and that he was considering divorce. Prosecutors also said she had bought four life insurance policies on him between 2015 and 2017 without his knowledge.

Her business was in trouble. A forensic accountant testified that she owed close to $8 million, part of it from the purchase of a large estate in Midway that she meant to resell. A former lawyer for her told CBS that she hoped to clear nearly $10 million on that property, and that heavy borrowing is normal in the house-flipping trade. Eric Richins argued with her about the purchase. Prosecutors put his estate at more than $4 million on the day he died. In a separate case, filed in June 2025 and not yet tried, she is accused of submitting doctored bank statements in mortgage applications from July 2021, writing bad cheques between August and December 2021, and spending a friend's down-payment money on other debts.

About a month before his death, according to the prosecution, she took out one more policy on him, worth $100,000. A juror noted that it used her business address and named her as beneficiary, and the jury found that she had forged his signature on it.

For about two years Kouri Richins had been seeing Josh Grossman, a handyman she met through her business. The jury saw affectionate text messages between them, one of which raised the idea of marriage after a divorce. Before Eric Richins died she had booked a romantic trip for the two of them to a resort in St. Martin for April 2022. Grossman, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, testified that she once asked him whether he had ever killed anyone and how it had made him feel. He said they never went on the trip, and that she ended the relationship. After her arrest he contacted Eric Richins' family, overcome, he told the court, with guilt about the affair.

Others recalled darker remarks. A neighbour testified that around Christmas 2021, after a fight with her husband, Kouri Richins told her it would be better if he were dead. One of Eric Richins' sisters told investigators that he had believed his wife tried to kill him on a trip to Greece several years earlier. The family's spokesman, Greg Skordas, said Eric had warned them to watch out for her if anything happened to him.

The prosecution's account of how the fentanyl reached the house came from Carmen Lauber, 54, who had cleaned the family's home for years through her aunt's cleaning business. In early 2022 she had just started a drug court programme and, she said, was still struggling with drug use. She testified that Kouri Richins asked her four times to buy pain pills, saying they were for an investor.

The first time, Lauber said, she got an envelope of opiate pills from a woman she knew. The second time Kouri Richins wanted "something stronger". Lauber said she found a man who had pills containing fentanyl and texted Kouri Richins, who replied, "Okay, go ahead and get them." She collected about $1,000 in cash left for her at a house in Midway that Kouri Richins was renovating, bought the pills at a petrol station on 11 February 2022, and buried them in the fire pit at that house. Around the end of February, she said, Kouri Richins asked for "some of the Michael Jackson stuff", and she bought more. The fourth purchase came after the death: three days after Eric Richins died, Kouri Richins texted her, "still have your hookup?", and later gave her a cheque for $1,300 marked "Construction clean Midway". "I never cleaned a house ever in my life for thirteen hundred dollars," Lauber said.

A few days after the death, Lauber testified, she spoke to Kouri Richins by phone. "Please tell me these pills were not for him," she said she told her. She said the reply was that Eric had died of a brain aneurysm. Phone records showed about 800 messages between the two women whose dates matched her timeline, although their contents had been deleted.

The defence went after her hard. Lauber's drug tests had come back positive for methamphetamine three times between late January and early March 2022. She first spoke to detectives in April 2023, when she faced new drug charges, and testified under immunity, as part of an agreement meant to spare her a long sentence on separate drug charges. In a recorded interview played in court one investigator explained that the help they wanted meant "give us the details that will ensure Kouri gets convicted of murder." The defence said she had first spoken of oxycodone and only later of fentanyl, and that she had first described three purchases, not four. The man she named as her supplier, Robert Crozier, testified that he never sold her fentanyl.

On 14 February 2022, three days after the first fentanyl purchase Lauber described, Eric Richins fell ill after eating a sandwich his wife had made for him. Court filings said he broke out in hives and had trouble breathing, and that he told a friend, "I think my wife tried to poison me." Prosecutors charged that meal as an attempted murder in March 2024. Questioned by the defence, Ali Staking, a friend of the couple, said they treated it at the time as an allergic reaction: he used an EpiPen, and the friends joked about not eating what Kouri served.

The defence said the couple were celebrating that evening because she was about to close on the biggest deal her company had ever done. Prosecutors said she served him a drink laced with fentanyl, either a Moscow mule or a lemon drop shot. In the account she wrote for police, her story began with that drink at about 9:15 p.m. Investigators found a note in a kitchen cabinet with the words "drink in bed", which prosecutors said described the killing. She told police she had gone to sleep in one of her sons' rooms and found her husband when she returned to bed. Prosecutors said the boy would have testified that she did not sleep in his room; the defence said what he told police at the time matched her account.

Her 911 call became evidence against her. The operator repeatedly asked her to put the phone on speaker and count out loud while she did chest compressions. A digital forensic analyst testified that the phone's proximity sensor showed she was holding it to her ear for the call, and one juror later said it did not sound as if much effort was going into the compressions. Texts she sent a friend afterwards described pumping on his chest and screaming at him to come back to life.

Within hours, Katie Richins-Benson testified, her sister-in-law was talking about selling the house and closing on the Midway estate. According to court filings, she signed the papers to complete the purchase the next day. Prosecutors also showed GIFs opened on her phone that morning that appeared to celebrate coming into money. Prosecutors showed searches she made after his death, among them "luxury prisons for the rich in america", how long life insurers take to pay out, and what a death certificate says when someone is poisoned. Her former lawyer said the searches came after police served a search warrant on the house, which made them understandable.

On 7 March 2023 she self-published "Are You With Me?", a picture book in which a boy learns to live with his father's death, initially written for her own children. On a Utah television programme she described their grief and said the death had been unexpected. On 8 May 2023 she was charged with her husband's murder and arrested. Ten days later prosecutors added fraud charges over life insurance policies worth some $2 million that, they said, she took out without his knowledge.

The case moved slowly. A judge refused her bail. In September 2023 prosecutors said a letter found in her cell, titled "Walk the Dog", set out false testimony for her mother and brother. Her first lawyer withdrew in May 2024 over an ethical conflict, and she was ordered to stand trial in August 2024. Her lawyers twice tried and failed to move the trial from Summit County, and the mortgage charges were split off for a later trial. Jury selection finished in February 2026.

Bloodworth opened on 23 February 2026 with a simple theory: "The evidence will prove that Kouri Richins murdered Eric for his money and to get a fresh start at life." Over three weeks the state called 40 witnesses. A toxicologist testified that tests found fentanyl in Eric Richins' body together with a related compound often present in illegally made fentanyl, and less than a normal dose of quetiapine, a medicine prescribed to his wife.

The defence argued that the investigation was "nothing but sloppy" and "driven by bias", shaped from the start by his family's conviction that she was guilty. Kathryn Nester told the jury that the cups were never tested, because the nanny put them in the dishwasher the next morning, and that no one could say how the fentanyl got into him. The defence pointed to his work-related knee and back pain, a trip he made to Mexico weeks before his death, and an empty hydrocodone bottle, expired in 2020, found by the bed. Prosecutors answered with police body-camera footage in which she assured an officer that her husband had never used illegal drugs.

After the state rested on 12 March, the defence rested too, without calling a witness. Kouri Richins told the judge she was waiving her right to testify on her lawyers' advice. Two jurors later told CBS they had been startled and disappointed, expecting to hear the rest of the story.

The jury of eight took about three hours. It found her guilty on all five counts. One juror told CBS he gave great weight to Lauber's testimony because the phone records backed it up, and that the jury saw her debts as the motive.

At sentencing the three boys, now in the care of Katie Richins-Benson, asked through statements read by counsellors for the heaviest sentence and said they would not feel safe if she were ever released. The defence asked for 25 years to life. Kouri Richins spoke for 30 to 40 minutes, by different accounts, mostly to her sons. "As much as you've been influenced into thinking that I'm a murderer, that I took your dad from you, that is completely wrong. That is an absolute lie," she said, and promised to fight on.

Mrazik said he had weighed both possible sentences and how the boys might feel about either one decades later. He described her crimes as an attempt to kill her husband followed by 17 days spent "doubling down" before trying again and succeeding, all for money. "A person convicted of those things is simply too dangerous to ever be free," he said. He imposed life without parole for the murder, five years to life for the attempted murder, one to 15 years on each fraud count and up to five years for forgery, all to run one after the other. Prosecutors asked for restitution of more than $1.3 million to two insurance companies. The judge gave her lawyers 28 days to file a motion for a new trial. Her separate financial case is still pending.
